C-123 describes (a) confirmContribution replaying a refunded/disputed row back to paid — identical to C-085 (same file/line actions.ts:181, same forever-valid-signature mechanism, same regrant via paidAt: { gt: birdPickedAt }), and (b) the webhook captured `status: { not: "paid" }` predicate resurrecting a reversed row — identical to C-084. No distinct mechanism, code site, or fix beyond those two. Marked duplicate of the earliest confirmContribution finding (C-085); its webhook half is covered by C-084.

merged.title: Razorpay refund/dispute arriving before the capture event is acknowledged with 200 and permanently lost
merged.reasoning: Confirmed and genuinely distinct from C-084 (different predicate, different fix). The reversal branch uses updateMany({ where: { id, status: "paid" }, data: { status: to } }) (route.ts:230-233). If a refund.processed / dispute.created arrives while the row is still 'created' (browser callback dead — the exact tab-death case this route exists for — and the payment.captured webhook delayed or mid-retry), moved.count is 0, the reversal is applied to nothing, and the handler returns NextResponse.json({ received: true }) unconditionally at route.ts:248, so Razorpay treats it as delivered and never resends. The writeAudit is inside `if (moved.count === 1)` (route.ts:234-238), so nothing records the dropped reversal. When the delayed payment.captured lands, the captured branch sets 'paid' and the money counts forever. Critically, C-084's fix (narrowing the captured predicate) does NOT fix this — the refund is dropped before it ever applies, so this needs its own fix. Downgraded Medium->Low: the window is narrow (refund must beat the capture webhook AND the browser callback must have died), but the consequence is a permanent, silent money-total lie.
merged.repro: Trace the three branches: for a 'created' row, refund.processed hits the else-branch (route.ts:222-233), updateMany where status:'paid' -> count 0 -> skips writeAudit -> falls to return 200 (route.ts:248). Razorpay (retries only on non-2xx, no ordering guarantee) never resends. Live: against test-mode keys deliver a signed refund.processed before payment.captured to the local route and read the row -> stays 'created', reversal lost; then deliver payment.captured -> 'paid'.
merged.fix: Make an early reversal durable: either return a non-2xx when the row is not-yet-paid so Razorpay retries after the capture lands, or persist a pending-reversal flag that the captured branch honours (a capture onto a pending-refund row lands 'refunded', not 'paid'). Also emit an audit line whenever a reversal is seen but not applied, so a dropped one is never silent.
merged.gate: Unit/integration test: refund.processed arriving before payment.captured ends with the row 'refunded' (or the event retried), never silently 'paid', and an audit entry exists.

merged.title: dismissMail read-then-delete race can delete a message another admin just requeued
merged.reasoning: Real check-then-act TOCTOU. dismissMail reads status at src/app/(main)/admin/mail/actions.ts:69-76 then deletes with no status condition: `prisma.outboundEmail.delete({ where: { id } })` (:78). retryMail four lines up (:45-48) does the correct thing — `updateMany({ where: { id, status: row.status }, ... })` conditioned on the read status. So dismissMail is the one write in this file that is NOT conditioned. If admin A retries row R (→queued) while admin B's dismiss sits between its read (saw 'failed') and its delete, B's delete removes the just-requeued row and a real email (often a corrected-address reset) is silently never sent. Reachability is the only limiter: it needs two admins acting on the same failed row within milliseconds; this app realistically has ~one admin (the owner), which is why it is Low, not why it is not-a-bug.
merged.repro: Code trace: actions.ts:78 `delete({ where: { id } })` carries no status guard, unlike retryMail's `updateMany({ where: { id, status: row.status } })` at :45-48. Interleave: A's retryMail commits status='queued' after B's findUnique (:69) read 'failed' but before B's delete (:78) fires; B's delete removes the requeued row.
merged.fix: Replace the unconditional delete with `deleteMany({ where: { id, status: 'failed' } })` and treat count===0 as 'that message moved on', mirroring retryMail's existing idiom in the same file.
merged.gate: Unit/integration test asserting dismissMail is a no-op (and returns the moved-on error) when the row's status is no longer 'failed' at delete time; or a regression assertion that the dismiss delete's WHERE includes status='failed'.

merged.title: Admin 'Retry' on a deferral-exhausted row creates an unkillable queued zombie that blackholes all future resets for that member
merged.reasoning: Verified against actual code. retryMail's write is `data: { status: "queued", attempts: 0, lastError: null, claimedAt: null }` (actions.ts:47) — it does NOT reset `deferrals` or `nextAttemptAt`. A row is retired to status='failed' with deferrals=MAX_DEFERRALS(10) by bookFailure's transient giveUp branch (email-queue.ts:256-274), and because transient failures decrement the attempt they consumed (:263), such a row can be 'failed' with attempts as low as 0. The drain's selection requires `deferrals: { lt: MAX_DEFERRALS }` (email-queue.ts:728), so after retryMail flips it back to 'queued' with deferrals still 10 the drain never selects it again. Compounding for kind='reset': it is foldable (email-queue.ts:447) and enqueueMail folds any queued/sending row of the same userId+kind and early-returns without draining (:449-459), so every later requestPasswordReset for that member folds into the zombie and returns {ok:true} while nothing is ever sent; the member can never receive another reset. dismissMail cannot clear it either — its guard is `row.status !== 'failed'` (:74) and the zombie is now 'queued'. verify rows escape because verificationMailState claims the row directly, bypassing the deferrals filter; reset/password-changed/deletion-scheduled have no such read-path. The retryMail docstring (:16-21) explains the attempts ceiling as 'a queue that will never look at it again' but is silent on the identical deferrals ceiling — a real comment-vs-code gap that is the root of this bug.
merged.repro: Rolled-back SQL on the shared DB: BEGIN; INSERT OutboundEmail kind='reset', status='failed', attempts=0, deferrals=10, userId=<u>; run retryMail(id) which sets status='queued', attempts=0, leaves deferrals=10; run the drain findFirst predicate (status='queued' AND kind IN reserved AND attempts<4 AND deferrals<10 AND due) -> 0 rows; run enqueueMail's fold SELECT (userId+kind, status IN ('queued','sending')) -> matches the zombie; ROLLBACK. Plus read of retryMail data object confirming deferrals/nextAttemptAt are absent.
merged.fix: retryMail must also reset `deferrals: 0` and `nextAttemptAt: null` so a provider-exhausted row becomes genuinely drain-eligible again; and correct the docstring to name the deferrals ceiling alongside the attempts ceiling.
merged.gate: Unit test: a row with deferrals=MAX_DEFERRALS and status='failed', after retryMail, satisfies the drain's exact selection predicate (attempts<MAX_ATTEMPTS AND deferrals<MAX_DEFERRALS AND due).

merged.title: enqueueMail's fold path returns before scheduleDrain, so pressing 'resend' never nudges a stuck queued row
merged.reasoning: Control flow confirmed: the fold branch returns at email-queue.ts:458 (`if (waiting) return { queued: true, id: waiting.id };`) before scheduleDrain() at :491, so a member's repeat requestPasswordReset (which folds — email-actions.ts:278-291) never re-nudges a stuck queued row. The stated design intent (comment at :481-491, the 2026-08-12 Nirad/Sanjula incident) is that enqueue nudges the drain to prevent stuck-queue waits; the fold path — the exact path 'resend' takes when a row already waits — skips that nudge. Downgraded from Medium to Low because the drain is GLOBAL (drains the whole queue, not the caller's rows), so recovery only fails to happen if BOTH the original after()-scheduled drain was lost AND no authenticated page view fires fleet-wide for a while; a stuck reset is picked up by the next authed page view by anyone. The harm window is a lost-drain coincidence during low IST-night traffic for a signed-out locked-out member. Real, narrow, clean one-line fix.
merged.repro: Structural early return at email-queue.ts:458 precedes scheduleDrain() at :491; nothing else drains from the unauthenticated reset pages, and requestPasswordReset re-submissions all fold.
merged.fix: Call scheduleDrain() before the fold-path return (or restructure enqueueMail so every return path nudges the drain).
merged.gate: Not strong; a test that the fold path still schedules a drain, or a comment tying the fold path to the same nudge invariant the create path documents.

merged.title: Dev drain with EMAIL_DEV_SEND=1 but no RESEND_API_KEY marks rows 'sent' off a console.log, violating the queue's own core invariant
merged.reasoning: Trace confirmed but scope is dev-only and owner-only. queueIsSendable's dev branch (email-queue.ts:130-146) requires EMAIL_DEV_SEND=1 and ADMIN_EMAIL but — unlike the production branch (:120-128) — never checks RESEND_API_KEY. With the key unset, the drain runs; it only selects rows addressed to ADMIN_EMAIL (localDrainRecipient scope, email-queue.ts:726). sendMail then falls through the EMAIL_DEV_SEND!=1 suppression (email.ts:170, skipped because the flag is 1) into the no-key non-production branch (:189-198), which prints and returns `{ ok: true }`; claimAndSend records status='sent' with sentAt on result.ok alone (:319-333), spending a real budget slot off a console.log — the exact invariant the 2026-08-12 fix established as inviolable. Kept Low because the config is self-contradictory (EMAIL_DEV_SEND=1 means 'really send' yet no key means 'cannot send'), it never touches a real member's mail (drain narrowed to the owner's own address), and .env normally carries the production key. Still a genuine, verifiable breach of a named invariant with a one-line fix, so worth closing.
merged.repro: Static branch trace across email-queue.ts:130-146, email.ts:170/189-198, and claimAndSend email-queue.ts:319-333. Live: NODE_ENV!=production, EMAIL_DEV_SEND=1, ADMIN_EMAIL set, RESEND_API_KEY unset; enqueue a verify to ADMIN_EMAIL, load a page, row flips to sent with sentAt and only a terminal print.
merged.fix: queueIsSendable's dev branch should also require RESEND_API_KEY (fail-closed, matching the production branch), or sendMail's no-key branch must return ok:false whenever EMAIL_DEV_SEND=1.
merged.gate: Unit test of queueIsSendable() returning false when EMAIL_DEV_SEND=1 and RESEND_API_KEY is unset.

merged.title: Dismissing a same-day-bounced row deletes its sentAt and hands back a phantom budget slot (B-071 regression vector)
merged.reasoning: Verified. dailyBudget counts off sentAt with no status filter (email-queue.ts:397-399), which is the deliberate B-071 fix (a bounce webhook flips status to 'failed' but sentAt is preserved — resend/webhook/route.ts:107-128 sets status='failed' and never clears sentAt). But dismissMail hard-deletes any 'failed' row (`prisma.outboundEmail.delete`, actions.ts:78), removing the row entirely — including one with a same-day sentAt the budget was counting. Deleting a same-UTC-day bounced row therefore hands back a slot Resend already counted, re-spending against the real 100/day quota. A single dismissal is harmless below the cap; >5 same-day bounce-dismissals eat the deliberate 95-vs-100 margin and push sends into hard rejections — B-071 resurrected through the admin button. Bounced rows do surface in the 'failed' worklist, and dismissing a dead address is the intended use, so the path is reachable; Low because it needs several same-day dismissals near the cap (most plausible on launch day).
merged.repro: Rolled-back SQL: SELECT count WHERE sentAt >= startOfUtcDay(); DELETE one OutboundEmail with sentAt >= today's UTC midnight and status='failed'; re-SELECT -> count dropped by 1. Webhook half confirmed at resend/webhook/route.ts:107-128 (status='failed', sentAt untouched).
merged.fix: dismissMail should not remove rows whose sentAt falls in the current UTC day (soft-clear the status instead of deleting, or retain sent-today rows), or make the daily budget an append-only ledger independent of row existence.
merged.gate: Rolled-back SQL assertion or unit test: dismissing a failed row that has a same-UTC-day sentAt leaves the sentAt-based budget count unchanged.

merged.title: A provider-quota-deferred verify row shows 'A link has been sent to your email' for up to 24 hours, with no resend button
merged.reasoning: Code trace of verificationMailState (email-queue.ts:843-913) holds. For a verify row status='queued' with nextAttemptAt set to the next UTC midnight (the quota-deferral path, bookFailure:268-270) while global budget.verifyRemaining>0: line 873 does not take the 'queued' answer (gated only on global arithmetic), `due` is false (:883) so the send is skipped, the fresh re-read is still 'queued' (:904-909), and the function returns 'imminent' (:913). The banner renders 'imminent' as 'A link has been sent to your email. Tap on it to verify your account.' and hides the resend button (verify-email-banner.tsx:193-201, 220-229), for up to ~24h, when nothing was ever accepted. The same 'has been sent' overstatement also shows during ordinary transient backoff windows (1-60 min) on a first-attempt provider hiccup. The state machine genuinely has no branch for 'row individually deferred to a future window while global arithmetic shows budget'. Low: the 24h case needs real drift between Resend's count and the local sentAt count (the margin usually absorbs it), and the row does eventually send at the next window; the transient-window overstatement is mild and self-correcting.
merged.repro: Deterministic trace of email-queue.ts:862-913 against status='queued', nextAttemptAt=next UTC midnight, verifyRemaining>0 -> returns {state:'imminent'}; verify-email-banner.tsx:193-201/220 renders 'A link has been sent' and omits the resend button.
merged.fix: Return {state:'queued', sendingAt: row.nextAttemptAt} (not 'imminent') when a queued row's nextAttemptAt is a budget-window deferral / sufficiently far in the future, so the copy stops asserting a completed send; or soften the 'imminent' banner copy away from 'has been sent'.
merged.gate: Unit test mapping a queued row with a far-future nextAttemptAt to a state whose copy does not assert a completed send.

merged.title: DRAIN_LEASE_MS (45s) is shorter than a worst-case pass (8 sends x 10s timeout ≈ 80s+), so the one-pass-at-a-time guarantee lapses exactly during provider brownouts
merged.reasoning: Arithmetic and control flow confirmed on committed constants. BATCH=8 (email-queue.ts:92) x SEND_TIMEOUT_MS=10_000 (email.ts:77) = 80s worst-case pass, well over DRAIN_LEASE_MS=45_000 (email-queue.ts:602). The lease is taken once in drainMailQueue (:660) and drainWithLease's loop (:704-744) never re-checks or renews it; takeDrainLease fences only on `expiresAt: { lte: now }` (:616-617), so expiry alone hands the lease over while the first pass is still alive and sending. During a Resend brownout (the exact B-072 condition the lease exists for) pass 1 runs ~80s, the lease lapses at 45s, a concurrent page-view after() takes it, and two-plus passes run in parallel — reopening the self-inflicted 429 storm and burning deferrals across rows faster. Per-row claims (claimAndSend conditional updateMany) still prevent same-row double-sends, so the damage is rate-storm + accelerated deferral burn, not duplicates — hence Medium (degradation under a provider-outage edge), not High. Corroborated by mail-policy.test.mjs:76 pinning ONE_PASS_MS=30_000 as 'the time one pass takes', which both the 45s lease and the 80s worst case contradict.
merged.repro: Constant arithmetic: email-queue.ts:92 (BATCH=8), email.ts:77 (SEND_TIMEOUT_MS=10_000), email-queue.ts:602 (DRAIN_LEASE_MS=45_000) -> 8x10s=80s>45s. drainWithLease (:704-744) has no lease renewal; takeDrainLease (:616-617) hands over on expiresAt<=now. Optional live sim: stub sendMail to sleep 10s with 8+ queued rows and two drainMailQueue calls 46s apart, observe both hold the lease.
merged.fix: Set DRAIN_LEASE_MS >= BATCH * SEND_TIMEOUT_MS + margin (e.g. match STALE_CLAIM_MS = 120_000), or renew/re-check the lease each loop iteration in drainWithLease.
merged.gate: Add a unit assertion importing the constants: DRAIN_LEASE_MS >= BATCH * SEND_TIMEOUT_MS (beside mail-policy.test.mjs's pass-timing assertions).

merged.title: sendMail's timeout race leaves the losing Resend promise unhandled - a late transport failure becomes an unhandled rejection
merged.reasoning: The central premise is factually wrong about JS/V8 semantics. Promise.race registers a reaction (via PerformPromiseThen) on EVERY input promise, so a rejection handler IS attached to `send` at email.ts:215 even after the timer wins the race — a later rejection of `send` runs race's internal reject reaction (a no-op because the result already settled) and is therefore 'handled', never surfacing to Node's unhandledRejection path. I proved this two ways: (1) an instrumented script with a process.on('unhandledRejection') listener where the late-rejecting loser fires NOTHING and node exits 0; (2) the finding's OWN exact proofPlan snippet `node -e "const p=new Promise((_,rej)=>setTimeout(rej,50)); Promise.race([p,new Promise(r=>setTimeout(()=>r(null),10))]).then(()=>{});"` which the finding claims 'exits 1 with an unhandled rejection' — it actually exits 0. Since there is no unhandled rejection, the entire chain (spurious Sentry capture / process termination / stranded 'sending' row) does not occur. This is a plausible-but-wrong finding of exactly the kind the validation step exists to kill.
merged.repro: Executed both the finding's exact snippet and an instrumented variant with an unhandledRejection listener; both exit 0 and the listener never fires, disproving the premise that the race loser's rejection is unhandled.

merged.title: Mail drain failure paths log to console only - a systematically failing drain never reaches Sentry
merged.reasoning: Verified as a real inconsistency with an established convention. reportSwallowed (src/lib/report-error.ts) exists explicitly for M09 — 'a guard that hides its own breakage is worse than no guard' — and routes swallowed errors to Sentry; it is used by catchups.ts:73 and retention.ts:105. The mail drain, a comparable near-every-page-view swallowed guard with no cron, uses bare console.error instead: scheduleDrain (email-queue.ts:527-540), scheduleSend (:512-525), and the (main) layout's after() backstop (layout.tsx:81-87) — the same layout where the Catch-up engine DOES use reportSwallowed. Additionally takeDrainLease's create-catch (:622-628) swallows ANY error (connection refused, a missing/drifted QueueLease table) as 'someone holds the lease'->null, so a structural failure reads as 'queue busy'. A pre-bookkeeping drain failure (takeDrainLease/dailyBudget throwing) then produces no Sentry event; the only witness is the admin panel's climbing 'waiting' count. Low because per-row send failures are well-booked and surface in mailHealth, and the gap only bites on structural failures — but it is a genuine, named-consequence violation of a convention this repo already adopted for its two other most-critical swallowed guards.
merged.repro: reportSwallowed defined in report-error.ts and used at catchups.ts:73 and retention.ts:105; email-queue.ts scheduleDrain:532 / scheduleSend:517 / layout.tsx:85 use bare console.error, and takeDrainLease:625-627 catches all errors as null. A drainMailQueue throw (e.g. QueueLease table absent) captures nothing in Sentry while pages render normally.
merged.fix: Route the drain-scheduling and lease failures through reportSwallowed('email', err, ...), and narrow takeDrainLease's create-catch to the unique-violation case (report/rethrow other errors instead of reading them as a held lease).
merged.gate: Not strong; optionally a test asserting the scheduleDrain/scheduleSend/lease catch paths call reportSwallowed.

merged.title: Mail-drain lease (45s) is shorter than a worst-case drain pass (~80s+), so concurrent passes resume exactly when Resend degrades
merged.reasoning: Same root cause and same anchor (email-queue.ts:602 DRAIN_LEASE_MS vs BATCH x SEND_TIMEOUT_MS) as C-108: the 45s drain lease is shorter than an ~80s worst-case pass under a Resend brownout, so the lease lapses mid-pass and concurrent passes resume, reopening the B-072 429 storm. Identical mechanism, arithmetic and fix direction. Canonical is C-108 (earliest id); validated fully there at Medium.

merged.title: The 730-day AdminMessage retention leaves AdminThread shells forever: subject text (member-written) outlives the transcript, and emptied threads render oddly
merged.reasoning: Verified: retention.ts:111-115 deletes prisma.adminMessage only; grep for `adminThread.delete`/`deleteMany` across src/ finds it nowhere in app code (only in the generated Prisma docstrings). AdminThread.member is Cascade (schema.prisma:658) and AdminMessage.thread is Cascade (schema.prisma:680) — child->parent only, so purging messages leaves the parent thread untouched. AdminThread.subject is member-derived (deriveSubject at messages/actions.ts:92) and persists indefinitely, so a ~90-char slice of the member's first message outlives the 2-year transcript the KEEP_DAYS.adminMessages=730 comment (retention.ts:31-32) says is 'not a permanent transcript'. Rendering confirmed: thread-list.tsx:76-77 emits `You: ` + previewOf(lastBody) with no guard for messageCount 0, and the '{n} messages' line hides at messageCount<=1 (line 80), so a fully-emptied thread renders as a bare subject + 'You:' over an empty preview. This is genuinely LATENT: the site is pre-release, so no thread is 730 days old yet and it cannot manifest for ~2 years. Admin/self-visible only.
merged.repro: Rolled-back proof per TRAPS.md: BEGIN; DELETE FROM "AdminMessage" WHERE "threadId"='<t>'; SELECT id, subject FROM "AdminThread" WHERE id='<t>'; ROLLBACK — the thread row and its member-derived subject survive. In the UI, loading that member's /messages renders the shell via ThreadList with lastBody '' and messageCount 0.
merged.fix: In the adminMessages sweep step, after deleting messages past the cutoff, also delete AdminThreads left with zero remaining messages (or whose lastMessageAt is past the window) so the subject residue and empty shells go with the transcript; alternatively exclude emptied threads from the member list query.
merged.gate: A retention unit/integration test asserting that a thread whose every message is past 730 days is removed (no orphaned AdminThread row) after runRetentionSweep.

merged.title: Retention sweep deletes AdminMessage rows without purging their screenshot bytes
merged.reasoning: Verified: AdminMessage.imageUrl exists and points at an uploaded R2 screenshot (schema.prisma:677 `imageUrl String? // one optional screenshot`). The sweep's adminMessages step (retention.ts:111-115) is a bare `prisma.adminMessage.deleteMany({ where: { createdAt: { lt: cutoff(730) } } })` — it never reads imageUrl and never queues into PendingImagePurge. Contrast: the account-purge path DELIBERATELY collects admin-thread screenshots (account-purge.ts:109-112 selects imageUrl from every message in the member's threads and createMany's them into PendingImagePurge at 266-269), proving the system treats these bytes as purge-worthy. Once the sweep deletes the rows, collectImageUrls can no longer enumerate them, so the R2 objects orphan permanently, unfindable — exactly the H9 class this subsystem exists to close. LATENT like C-062 (needs a 730-day-old message), but the consequence is a permanent privacy residue of members' personal screenshots to admins, which the retention docs frame as a GDPR Art.5(1)(e) obligation.
merged.repro: Read-only: any AdminMessage row with imageUrl IS NOT NULL will, at its 730-day mark, be deleted by the sweep with its R2 object left behind and no row naming it. Code trace: retention.ts:112 deleteMany vs account-purge.ts:109-112 + 266-269 which the sweep omits.
merged.fix: Make the adminMessages step a transaction that findMany's the due rows' imageUrls, pendingImagePurge.createMany's the non-null ones (reason:'retention'), then deleteMany — the same collect-then-delete shape declinePhoto/deletePost/purge use.
merged.gate: Test asserting the adminMessages sweep step enqueues each deleted message's imageUrl into PendingImagePurge before deleting the row.

merged.title: Grace-period purge races sign-in cancellation: account erased after the member cancelled
merged.reasoning: Verified TOCTOU. The sweep reads the due list once (retention.ts:225-238, WHERE deletionRequestedAt < cutoff(60)) then loops purgeUserAccount(row.id) sequentially (240). purgeUserAccount's transaction (account-purge.ts:261-290) calls tx.user.delete at 281 with NO condition on deletionRequestedAt. Meanwhile a sign-in during the grace window IS the cancel gesture and is AWAITED: auth.ts:202-206 clears deletionRequestedAt to null (and the comment at 199-201 explicitly says 'signing someone in while their purge date still stands is the one wrong outcome here'). Because the purge tx runs READ COMMITTED with no predicate on the column, the interleaving sign-in's committed UPDATE conflicts with nothing, so a member who signs in between the findMany and their turn in the loop is purged anyway — irreversible loss of rows and R2 bytes after the product told them the deletion was cancelled. Window: sequential loop of up to PURGE_BATCH=10 purges (each up to a 30s tx), so minutes; even a 1-account batch has the findMany->purge gap. Rare (dormant-60-day account signing in during the ~02:30 IST nightly window) but genuine data loss on a user-protective path.
merged.repro: Per TRAPS.md rolled-back proof: with a throwaway user whose deletionRequestedAt is in the past, BEGIN; UPDATE that user SET deletionRequestedAt = NULL; then run the purge's DELETE FROM "User" WHERE id=<u> and observe it succeeds regardless of the cleared column; ROLLBACK. Code trace: retention.ts:226 is the only deletionRequestedAt filter; account-purge.ts:281 is unconditional.

merged.title: collectImageUrls' in-transaction claim is false under READ COMMITTED: a concurrent upload's bytes leak forever
merged.reasoning: The comment at account-purge.ts:82-84 claims image URLs are 'read INSIDE the purge transaction so nothing uploaded between the reading and the delete can slip past.' Verified the transaction sets NO isolationLevel (account-purge.ts:289 passes only `{ timeout: 30_000, maxWait: 5_000 }`), so it runs Postgres default READ COMMITTED, where each statement takes a fresh snapshot. A Post/Photo/CatchupEntry inserted+committed by a concurrent transaction AFTER collectImageUrls' SELECTs (264) but BEFORE tx.user.delete (281) is seen and cascade-deleted by the delete's newer snapshot, while its image URL was never collected -> orphaned R2 bytes with no row naming them (the exact H9 leak). The claim would only hold under REPEATABLE READ/Serializable (where the delete would fail serialization on the conflict) or with a lock on the user row before collecting. So this is a genuine comment-contradicts-code + latent leak. Downgraded to Low: reachable only on the admin-delete path (an admin deleting an actively-posting member — the retention path's members are dormant) and only in the sub-second multi-statement window; the harm is orphaned storage/privacy residue, not member-facing breakage.

Code: no isolationLevel at account-purge.ts:289; collect at 264, delete at 281.
merged.fix: Set the purge transaction's isolationLevel to 'RepeatableRead' (the delete then aborts on a conflicting concurrent insert and Prisma retries) OR lock/delete the User row first so FK KEY-SHARE locks make concurrent inserts fail, then collect. Also correct the comment to state the isolation it actually relies on.

merged.title: drainPendingImagePurges can throw P2025 from its failure branch when a concurrent drain deleted the row
merged.reasoning: Verified the asymmetric guard. In drainPendingImagePurges the success/delete branch is guarded — `prisma.pendingImagePurge.delete(...).catch(() => {})` with the comment 'Row already taken by a concurrent drain' (account-purge.ts:331-334) — but the failure branch's `prisma.pendingImagePurge.update({ where: { id: row.id }, ... })` (338-341) has NO catch, and Prisma `update` throws P2025 when the where matches nothing. Two drains can hold the same row: the sweep's unfiltered findMany (retention.ts:272 -> drainPendingImagePurges() take 500) and a scoped drain from deletePost (feed/actions.ts:82 `drainPendingImagePurges(urls)`, after the row is already committed-deleted at line 78) or purge (account-purge.ts:298). If drain A gets delImage=true and deletes row X while drain B independently gets delImage=false (a transient R2 error on the same key — delImageByKey returns false only on a non-ENOENT throw, storage.ts:248, since an already-deleted object returns 204/true at 238), B's unguarded update on the now-gone row X throws P2025. In the sweep it's absorbed by step() (retention.ts:97-99); in deletePost/collection-delete it rejects the server action AFTER the post is gone, so the member gets a failure toast for a delete that succeeded. Low: narrow race (concurrent drains on the same row + split R2 outcome), but a genuine unguarded error path the delete branch already models.
merged.repro: Unit sim: stub delImage to return false and prisma.pendingImagePurge.update to throw {code:'P2025'}, call drainPendingImagePurges([url]) and observe the rejection propagates. Code: guarded delete at account-purge.ts:331 vs bare update at 338-341.
merged.fix: Give the failure branch the same protection as the delete branch: append `.catch(() => {})` to the update, or switch it to `pendingImagePurge.updateMany({ where: { id: row.id }, ... })` which no-ops on zero matches.
merged.gate: Unit test: delImage=false + update throwing P2025 must not reject drainPendingImagePurges.

merged.title: loadDirectoryPage server action has no rate limit and no length cap on filter strings, unlike every sibling lookup endpoint
merged.reasoning: The mechanism is factually true — loadDirectoryPage (actions.ts) imports no rate-limit module and buildDirectoryWhere applies escapeLike but no length truncation — but the claimed stability/DoS consequence does not hold, so this is 'right about the mechanism, wrong about the consequence' (TRAPS). (1) The queries run over the ~2,000-row User table (audit's own '2k headroom'), not a large table; a 100KB/1MB ILIKE '%pattern%' fails FAST per row because the pattern is longer than the short name/workplace/jobTitle fields, and the places EXISTS is over an equally small UserPlace table. Postgres LIKE has no catastrophic backtracking. So per-call cost is modest and independent of pattern length. (2) The action is auth-gated (requireVerifiedEmail, actions.ts:63) so only verified members reach it, addressing the M1 harvest concern the same way the endpoints do. (3) The equivalent GET (DirectoryPage) runs SEVEN queries in Promise.all with the same uncapped URL filters and no rate limit; a member can already scroll/scrape the whole roll, so adding a throttle only to the action would be inconsistent without closing any real hole. No concrete pool-saturation or instance-degradation scenario survives scrutiny. The residual (defense-in-depth length cap on a 25MB-body action) is a hygiene nicety, not a pre-release bug.
merged.repro: n/a — refuted.

merged.title: /api/places/search has no length cap on q, unlike the M44 cap on its sibling
merged.reasoning: Mechanism true (places/search route.ts:89 trims but does not length-cap q before building prefix/contains patterns), but the DoS consequence does not hold. (1) The rate limit IS present: rateLimit('search', ...) at route.ts:84, 120/min per verified account. (2) A long LIKE pattern is CHEAP, not expensive: the prefix arms use the btree lower() indexes and an 8-16KB prefix matches essentially nothing (returns fast); the only sequential arm is altNames ILIKE '%pattern%', gated to q>=4 chars, and a long needle fails immediately on every short altNames string (needle longer than haystack) — Postgres LIKE has no catastrophic backtracking. So the 234k-row scan cost is fixed by ROW COUNT (an inherent, documented cost the comment at route.ts:81-83 already owns) and is NOT amplified by pattern length; capping length changes nothing about it. The M44 analogy is misleading: M44 capped users/search because its per-WORD ILIKE conjunction (one AND-clause per token) grew unboundedly — places/search has a fixed 3-5 clause query with no per-word split, so that mechanism is absent. No concrete stability consequence survives; the cap is defense-in-depth hygiene, not a bug.
merged.repro: n/a — refuted.

merged.title: Signup accepts batchYear earlier than yearLeft — the impossible pair the profile editor refuses
merged.reasoning: Verified the asymmetry. signupSchema (validators.ts:59-97) has no cross-field check that batchYear >= yearLeft — its only refines are 'alumni need all three years', 'teachers need yearJoined', and fullNameFits. registerUser (auth/actions.ts:77-93) cross-checks ONLY yearLeft < yearJoined, then derives batchType = batchTypeFromLeaving(yearLeft, batchYear). batchTypeFromLeaving (utils.ts:402-419) explicitly returns null when batchYear < yearLeft, with a comment stating that pair 'is the two fields swapped at signup' (audit Low 110). The profile editor's yearClash (profile-actions.ts:239-241) refuses exactly this pair ('Your batch year cannot be before the year you left'). So signup stores the impossible pair the editor refuses: batchYear=2005 + yearLeft=2010 (both individually calendar-valid; batchYear allows ahead:7) passes, batchType is silently written null. Confirmed cross-field validation asymmetry between the two writers. Medium: it requires the member to type the two fields swapped (self-inflicted), affects only that one row (batchType null -> excluded from batch-targeted content and mis-joins the batch group), and is silently unfixable-except-by-careful-reorder, but there is no corruption of other members' data.

The profile then prints 'Batch 2005' beside years ...-2010, and the same pair is rejected if the member later tries to save it in the profile editor.

Best placed as a shared cross-field check imported by both the signup path and yearClash so the two cannot drift.
merged.gate: A unit test on the shared clash rule asserting (batchYear=2005, yearLeft=2010) is refused, exercised by both the signup validation path and profile yearClash.

merged.title: The layout's after() drain costs ~9 OutboundEmail/QueueLease queries including 3 writes on every authenticated page view even when the queue is empty
merged.reasoning: Mechanism verified; consequence downgraded. In production queueIsSendable() returns true whenever RESEND_API_KEY is set (email-queue.ts:118-128), so layout.tsx:81-87's after() drain runs on every authenticated page view. With an empty queue drainMailQueue issues: takeDrainLease updateMany on the single 'mail-drain' QueueLease row (612-619, a write that matches 1 every time because releaseDrainLease sets expiresAt=new Date(0) at 634, leaving the row permanently 'expired'), then drainWithLease (676-748) does reclaim updateMany (682), dailyBudget twice = 4 counts (693 and loop-iter 705, each dailyBudget is 2 parallel counts at 397-400), findFirst (713) -> null -> break, final count (746), and releaseDrainLease updateMany (632-634). ~9 statements incl. 3 writes per view, all with no cheap emptiness precheck — confirmed. Downgraded to Low because it runs inside after() (no user-visible latency), the statements are serialized (never 9 concurrent on the 5-conn pool), and single-row updates on one QueueLease row are trivial for Postgres; the finder's 'resource-exhaustion / hard-down at scale' framing is overstated. The concrete, nameable cost is real but modest: measurable DB write load + extended Vercel function duration on the hottest path, 99% of the time doing nothing. The loser-path failing INSERT only occurs during true after()-overlap while a winner still holds the ~45s lease, which for a fast empty drain is a small window, so it is rarer than the finding implies.
merged.repro: Enable Prisma query logging in a production-semantics run; load one authenticated page with an empty OutboundEmail queue; count statements attributable to the after() tick: expect takeDrainLease updateMany (matched 1), reclaim updateMany, 4 counts from two dailyBudget calls, one findFirst returning null, one final queued count, and releaseDrainLease updateMany.
merged.fix: Add a single cheap precheck at the top of drainMailQueue after queueIsSendable(): count({where:{status:'queued'}}) (an indexed count) and return early when 0, before takeDrainLease/reclaim/budget. That collapses the empty-queue case (the overwhelming majority) from ~9 statements/3 writes to 1 read. Optionally stop having releaseDrainLease set expiresAt to epoch so the lease is not re-taken on literally every view.
merged.gate: A test that counts Prisma calls from drainMailQueue against an empty queue and asserts it performs no lease write when nothing is queued.

merged.title: Production's daily /api/demo/reset cron GET is redirected to /login by the proxy — the carefully-built 200 no-op branch is unreachable, defeating its own stated purpose
merged.reasoning: Code trace confirms the route's no-op branch is unreachable on production. vercel.json ships the '0 20 * * *' cron for /api/demo/reset to both projects (lines 10-13). On the production build IS_DEMO is false, so proxy.ts skips the demo branch (110-125); requestHost is not LEGACY_HOST; sessionCookie is absent; pathname is not '/' or '/groups'; and /api/demo/reset is NOT in publicPaths (203-247) — its two sibling crons /api/catchups/tick (240) and /api/retention/sweep (244) ARE listed with comments that they exist 'only to get past the redirect-to-login', but this one was forgotten. So isPublic=false and the !sessionCookie branch (256-265) answers a 307 redirect to /login?next=%2Fapi%2Fdemo%2Freset. The route GET's `if (!IS_DEMO) return NextResponse.json({ok:true,skipped})` (route.ts:86-91) never runs, contradicting both its comment and docs/spec/demo.md. merged.repro: curl -sI https://rishivalley.space/api/demo/reset (GET, no cookie, no auth header) returns HTTP 307 with Location /login?next=%2Fapi%2Fdemo%2Freset, not the intended 200 JSON {ok:true,skipped:'not the demo deployment'}. The redirect is emitted by proxy.ts:264 because publicPaths lacks the path.

merged.gate: Extend the proxy/security-regressions test to assert /api/demo/reset with no cookie is treated as public (next(), not a /login redirect), matching its two sibling cron routes.

merged.title: First-open race on /notice/[id] still mints duplicate admin threads (the exact M46 failure, incompletely fixed)
merged.reasoning: Verified the TOCTOU and the comment-vs-code drift. notice/[id]/page.tsx resolves a legacy admin_note notification by findFirst on (memberId, kind:'notice', createdAt) (54-61), then, if null, calls openAdminNoticeThread (admin-threads-server.ts:94-118) which is a plain prisma.adminThread.create — not an upsert. AdminThread (schema) has only reportId @unique; there is NO @@unique on (memberId, kind, createdAt), confirmed by grepping the model. Under READ COMMITTED two concurrent first-opens both read null and both create, then both run notification.update (71-74) last-write-wins, leaving one linked thread and one orphaned thread visible in /messages and the admin inbox. The comment block (41-53) explicitly presents this as fixed ('two requests arriving together ... both minted a thread' described as the OLD behavior), but the deterministic key is only idempotent if backed by a unique constraint or an upsert, and neither exists — the fix only made SEQUENTIAL revisits idempotent (via the link-rewrite short-circuit at 37 and findFirst catching an already-created thread on a later visit). Confirmed defect. Downgraded to Low: reachability is narrow (only LEGACY admin_note notifications whose link does not yet start with /messages/, opened by two truly-simultaneous requests), and the harm is a duplicate conversation thread (no data loss, recoverable), not corruption.
merged.repro: Against a test account holding an unresolved admin_note notification (link not starting with /messages/), fire two concurrent authenticated GETs to /notice/<id>; count AdminThread rows where memberId=<test> AND kind='notice' AND createdAt=<notification.createdAt> — 2 rows reproduces the race the comment claims is impossible.

Fix the comment if the constraint route is declined.
merged.gate: A rolled-back concurrency test (two parallel resolves against one notification) asserting exactly one AdminThread row results; and a schema test pinning the unique index once added.

merged.title: getWordleAnswer has no fetch deadline: a hanging NYT endpoint blocks the /dark-mode render instead of reaching the fallback
merged.reasoning: Verified. wordle.ts:36-40 calls fetch(`https://www.nytimes.com/svc/wordle/v2/${key}.json`, { next: { revalidate: 3600 } }) with no signal/AbortSignal.timeout. The try/catch (35-49) only catches a REJECTION; a slow failure (connection accepted, response never arriving) does not reject within the render budget, so the await hangs until the platform kills the function. dark-mode/page.tsx:29 does `await getWordleAnswer()` directly in the server render path, so /dark-mode would return 5xx/504 for the first visitor after each cache expiry during an NYT hang rather than degrading to FALLBACK_WORDS (16), contradicting the file header's promise that any NYT failure keeps the gate functional. Confirmed as an unbounded external call in a render path. Downgraded to Low: /dark-mode is a niche settings gauntlet (not a core surface), the trigger is a specific NYT hang (fast failures already reach the fallback), and once any single fetch succeeds the 1h data cache shields subsequent visitors; worst case is a member temporarily unable to enable dark mode.
merged.repro: Code trace: the fetch options object at wordle.ts:36-40 has no signal, and the catch at 47 only fires on rejection; a hung socket does not reject inside the page's budget. Demonstrable with the same fetch shape against a non-routable address (10.255.255.1) exceeding the function budget vs. the same call with AbortSignal.timeout(3000) reaching the fallback.
merged.fix: Add signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3000) (or similar) to the fetch options so a slow/blackholed NYT endpoint aborts and the catch returns FALLBACK_WORDS.
merged.gate: A unit test that mocks fetch to hang and asserts getWordleAnswer() resolves to a FALLBACK_WORDS value within the timeout budget.

merged.title: A stale or revoked session cookie drops the deep link: (main) layout redirects to /login without the ?next= the proxy preserves
merged.reasoning: Verified the two-gate asymmetry. proxy.ts appends next=pathname+search ONLY on the no-cookie branch (256-264). When a session cookie is present but auth() rejects it, the request passes the proxy's presence check (149-151) and reaches the (main) layout, where `if (!session?.user) redirect('/login')` (layout.tsx:24-26) redirects with NO next param. Per the stack facts auth() returns null for a revoked/blocked/deleted session (credentialVersion mismatch), so a member whose other-device cookie was invalidated by a password reset/block — a designed, recurring state — following a shared deep link (/letters/<id>) is bounced to bare /login and lands on /feed after re-auth, losing the link the B-022 fix (proxy.ts:263) preserves for the no-cookie case. The layout already has the path in hand (x-pathname via currentPath(), 147-150). Confirmed inconsistent handling of the same 'needs login' case across the two gates. Low: UX-only degradation (lost deep link after re-auth) on a stale/revoked-cookie member. Note the pure-expiry sub-case is weaker (an expired cookie is usually dropped by the browser, hitting the no-cookie branch that DOES add next); the reliable trigger is credentialVersion revocation, which leaves an unexpired-but-invalid cookie.
merged.repro: On a test account, reset the password from another session (bumps credentialVersion) so the browser still holds an unexpired-but-invalid authjs.session-token; open /letters/<id>; observe the (main) layout redirect to /login with no next param; sign in; land on /feed instead of the letter.
merged.fix: In layout.tsx replace redirect('/login') with redirect('/login?next=' + encodeURIComponent(path)) using the x-pathname already read for touchLastSeen, matching proxy.ts's B-022 behavior.
merged.gate: An e2e/integration test that seeds an invalid-but-present session cookie, requests a deep link under (main), and asserts the Location carries next=<deep link>.

merged.title: viewport themeColor is hard-coded to the light background, so dark-theme members get warm-paper browser chrome around a charcoal app
merged.reasoning: Verified. src/app/layout.tsx exports a STATIC `viewport` object with themeColor:'#E4E1D5' (50-53), the light --background. The same file reads the per-request theme cookie (68) and drives ThemeProvider defaultTheme={theme}, so a dark-theme member's <html> renders class='dark' with .dark --background #1C2420 (per globals.css, dark shipped 2026-08-02), but the emitted <meta name='theme-color'> stays the light token — a static export cannot read the cookie. So on iOS a dark-theme member gets warm-paper Safari chrome around a charcoal app, the exact mismatch the constant's own comment (44-49) exists to prevent, inverted. grep confirms this is the only themeColor in src. manifest.ts carries the same fixed value (defensible for an install splash). Confirmed. Low: cosmetic, iOS-only, dark-theme members only. A media-query themeColor array would be WRONG here because dark is cookie/class-driven with enableSystem=false, not prefers-color-scheme; the correct fix is generateViewport reading the cookie.
merged.repro: As a dark-theme test account, view document head: <meta name='theme-color' content='#E4E1D5'> while <html class='dark'> renders the #1C2420 background. Visually the Safari toolbar/status bar shows light paper around the dark page.
merged.fix: Replace the static `viewport` export with `export async function generateViewport()` that awaits getThemeCookie() (already imported/used in the layout) and returns themeColor '#1C2420' when dark, '#E4E1D5' otherwise. Do NOT use a prefers-color-scheme media array, since theme is cookie-driven.
merged.gate: A unit test on generateViewport asserting it returns the dark token when the theme cookie is 'dark' and the light token otherwise.

merged.title: PostHog config comment promises input-content masking that the two lines under it do not implement
merged.reasoning: Verified the comment/config mismatch (a guard that does not guard). posthog-provider.tsx:87-89 comment says the block adds a 'belt and braces ... never transmit the contents of an input' layer, but the two options under it are mask_all_element_attributes:false (90) and mask_personal_data_properties:true (91). mask_all_element_attributes:false is literally the NON-masking setting (leaves element-attribute capture on), and mask_personal_data_properties governs personal data in event/campaign PROPERTIES (URLs, referrers), not element/input content. Neither implements input-content masking; the option that would (mask_all_text, plus flipping mask_all_element_attributes to true) is absent. Per the brief, a comment claim that disagrees with the code beside it is itself the finding. Confirmed as documentation/config drift. Low, and NOT a live data leak: posthog-js autocapture already excludes input/textarea/select VALUES by its own defaults regardless of these options, so the real input protection exists — just not where this comment claims it does. The stated risk is latent (a future posthog default change would find the believed second layer absent).
merged.repro: Read the two option values against posthog-js semantics: mask_all_element_attributes:false = attributes captured (opposite of masking); mask_personal_data_properties = property-level personal-data masking, not element content; mask_all_text is not set. The comment's promised input-content masking is therefore not implemented by these lines.
merged.fix: Either correct the comment to describe what these two options actually do (property masking + attribute capture left on) and note that input-value safety rests on posthog-js autocapture defaults, or, if a genuine belt-and-braces layer is wanted, add mask_all_text:true and set mask_all_element_attributes:true.
merged.gate: A small assertion/test over the posthog config object pinning whichever intent is chosen (e.g. mask_all_text present) so the comment and config cannot drift again.

merged.title: skipTrailingSlashRedirect is global but the proxy reinstates no trailing-slash handling, so every trailing-slash URL 404s
merged.reasoning: The imagined mechanism (route resolution 404s on a trailing slash) is contradicted by the installed Next source. skipTrailingSlashRedirect:true (next.config.ts:199) only suppresses the client-facing 308 redirect; it does NOT disable internal trailing-slash normalization for route MATCHING (that is the separate skipProxyUrlNormalize flag, which this project does not set). In node_modules/next/dist/server/lib/router-utils/filesystem.js, fsChecker.getItem strips the trailing slash before matching the filesystem routes: `if (itemPath !== '/' && itemPath.endsWith('/')) itemPath = itemPath.substring(0, itemPath.length - 1)` (389-391), and base-server.js additionally runs removeTrailingSlash on urlPathname/resolvedUrlPathname before component matching (1410-1411). So /feed/ normalizes to /feed and is served 200 (no redirect, no 404) — which is the entire purpose of the flag: serve both forms without redirecting so the slash-sensitive /ingest rewrite is preserved. The Next doc example the finder cites is a trailingSlash:true (slash-ADDING) migration scenario, not evidence of a 404. No trailing-slash 404 exists; refuted.
merged.repro: filesystem.js:389-391 strips the trailing slash inside getItem regardless of skipTrailingSlashRedirect, so /feed/ resolves to the /feed appFile output; base-server.js:1410-1411 removeTrailingSlash confirms the same at the render layer.

merged.title: Unauthenticated /_next/image plus the *.r2.dev wildcard remotePattern is an open image-optimization amplifier billed to the owner
merged.reasoning: Verified. next.config.ts remotePatterns includes { protocol:'https', hostname:'*.r2.dev' } (213-216) with no pathname restriction, and proxy.ts's matcher excludes _next/image (322) with no other auth guard on the endpoint (grep confirms), so /_next/image is reachable anonymously. Because pub-<hash>.r2.dev public buckets are free and self-serve on the r2.dev suffix, an attacker can host arbitrarily large images on their own bucket and drive /_next/image?url=https://pub-<attacker>.r2.dev/<unique>.png&w=<size> in a loop; each unique source URL is a fresh fetch+decode+transform on the owner's Vercel image-optimization quota/billing. Next 16 clamps w/q, which caps output dimensions but NOT the per-unique-source billing/CPU dimension the attack exploits. next/image is actively used (bird-avatar.tsx:665 routes member photoUrl through it; also login/signup), so quota exhaustion also degrades legitimate avatars. Critically, the project's own upload-shared.ts pins the ONE historical host 'https://pub-a656209a5438484f9694738260255a5e.r2.dev' (line 80) with a comment: 'The exact host, not a pub-*.r2.dev wildcard: a wildcard would vouch for [any bucket]' — so the remotePatterns wildcard directly contradicts the codebase's own deliberate exact-host discipline. Confirmed cost/DoS amplifier. Medium: anonymous and reachable, but the impact is owner billing / image-opt quota exhaustion (a stability/cost degradation), not member data loss or a hard-down.
merged.repro: Signed out, request /_next/image?url=https://pub-<any-r2.dev-host>/x.png&w=640 — the optimizer accepts the host because remotePatterns matches *.r2.dev, then fetches and transforms attacker-chosen bytes. Looping unique url values forces fresh transformations against the owner's Vercel quota with no account required.
merged.fix: Replace the { hostname:'*.r2.dev' } remotePattern with the single historical host pinned in upload-shared.ts:80 (pub-a656209a5438484f9694738260255a5e.r2.dev), matching that file's deliberate exact-host choice. Optionally tighten the img-src/connect-src '*.r2.dev' CSP wildcards to the same exact host.
merged.gate: A next.config test asserting no image remotePattern uses a wildcard r2.dev hostname (only the exact legacy host or images.rishivalley.space), pinned alongside the existing security-regressions suite.

merged.title: Permissions-Policy payment=() may block PaymentRequest-based methods (Google Pay / UPI intent) inside Razorpay checkout
merged.reasoning: The header is real and its inheritance semantics are sound, but the scenario is unverifiable from code. next.config.ts:117 sets Permissions-Policy payment=() on /:path* (128), which per spec disables the W3C Payment Request API for the document AND all nested browsing contexts regardless of any iframe allow attribute. Razorpay checkout is loaded via checkout.js and opened with `new Razorpay(options)` (support-contribute.tsx:80,192), i.e. an injected modal iframe that IS a nested context of rishivalley.space, so payment=() would govern it — and the header comment 'Powerful features nothing here uses' is factually contradicted by the site integrating a payment provider. What cannot be settled from code: (a) whether Razorpay's checkout actually invokes new PaymentRequest() for its Google Pay / UPI-intent flows (it may use a redirect/popup or the Google Pay JS API path instead), and (b) whether real contributors use those specific methods. The 'Confirmed working in production 2026-08-05' comment covers card/netbanking/UPI-QR (which do not need the API). Card/UPI-QR remain as fallbacks, so even if confirmed the impact is a missing convenience method on Android, not broken payments. Defaulting to NEEDS-LIVE per the brief's skepticism rule; needs a real device.

merged.title: Catch-up 'days left' disagrees across surfaces: index/status/reminders count 24h blocks, answer page counts valley calendar days
merged.reasoning: Verified the lib-level split. daysUntilLabel (catchups.ts:700-708) computes days = Math.ceil(diff/DAY_MS) — a 24h-duration count — and feeds editionCountdownLabel (711-722) and describeEditionStatus (724-751). Those render member-facing on the /catchups index (page.tsx:164, via describeEditionStatus) and the Catch-up home masthead ([catchupId]/page.tsx:371, via editionCountdownLabel), plus not-yet-published.tsx. The daily reminder copy (catchups-notify.ts:194-196) uses `days` from daysLeftUntil (catchups.ts:186-193), also Math.ceil duration. Meanwhile the answer page's closesLabel (answer/page.tsx:56-69) counts valleyDaysBetween (utils.ts:669-673) — valley CALENDAR days — a deliberate audit-Low-28 fix commented at 60-64. So for answersCloseAt = 07:30 IST on day D: at ~20:00 IST on D-1, diff ~11.5h -> daysUntilLabel='last day' / daysLeftUntil=1 -> bell 'Last day to answer', while valleyDaysBetween(D,D-1)=1 -> answer page 'Answers close tomorrow.' And every morning 00:00-07:30 IST the card reads one higher (ceil crosses at the anchor hour, calendar count crosses at valley midnight). No code comment or bugs.md entry marks the index/masthead/reminder as intentionally duration-based; audit Low 28 was applied only to the answer page. Genuine member-visible contradiction one click apart, across three surfaces including the bell.
merged.repro: Unit: daysUntilLabel({answersCloseAt:'2026-03-11T02:00:00Z'}, now='2026-03-10T14:30:00Z' [20:00 IST D-1]) -> diff ~11.5h -> Math.ceil<=1 -> 'last day'. valleyDaysBetween(new Date('2026-03-11T02:00:00Z'), new Date('2026-03-10T14:30:00Z')) -> valleyDayStart(D-1) to valleyDayStart(D) = 1 -> answer page 'Answers close tomorrow.' Second case: now='2026-03-09T21:30:00Z' [03:00 IST], answersCloseAt='2026-03-11T02:00:00Z' -> ceil(52.5h/24)=3 'days left' vs valleyDaysBetween=2.
merged.fix: Route daysUntilLabel / editionCountdownLabel / describeEditionStatus and the reminder text through valley calendar-day counting (the same valleyDaysBetween conversion closesLabel already uses) so every countdown surface agrees. Note daysLeftUntil is ALSO used to seed the reminder daily bucket (answeringPatch:474, extendPhasePatch:499) and to key dueReminder — the safe change is to fix only the member-visible STRINGS to valley days and leave the bucket arithmetic, or unify both consistently; do not silently change bucket keying while touching the copy.
merged.gate: Unit test asserting daysUntilLabel/editionCountdownLabel agree with the answer page's closesLabel for an answersCloseAt anchored at a cron instant, swept across `now` values that straddle both valley-midnight and the anchor hour.

merged.title: Cron-anchored catch-up deadlines land inside the next tick's jitter window; a quiet group's phase slips a full day roughly half the time
merged.reasoning: Mechanism verified. advanceDueCatchups sets now=new Date() at the tick's invocation (catchups.ts:1153) and threads it through; answeringPatch (470) mints answersCloseAt = addDays(now, 7) = exact instant now+7*24h, preparingPatch (509-510) anchors publishAt = answersCloseAt+24h, addCadenceGap(now,...) (957) sets nextOpensAt. computeStatus fires a transition only when t >= m exactly (381-385). The cron (vercel.json '0 2 * * *') exists and calls advanceDueCatchups() unscoped (api/catchups/tick/route.ts). Because the deadline is anchored to the day-0 tick's jitter offset and the day-N tick fires at its own independent jitter offset, P(day-N offset < day-0 offset) ~ 50% for ANY non-zero, run-to-run jitter (magnitude irrelevant — even a sub-second earlier fire defers the transition a full day to the next tick). The lazy layout tick (advanceDueCatchups(userId), scope 1156) only heals groups where SOME member loads a page, so a fully dormant group can run a phase up to ~1 day long and its cadence drifts later. Real and code-provable. Downgraded to Low: heavy preconditions (a group where literally no member loads any authed page across the whole miss window AND the cron is actually active — CRON_SECRET is still owed by the owner, so the cron currently 401s), self-heals on any visit, consequence is soft timing (a phase ~1 day long) within the spec's lazy-advance model, no data loss.
merged.repro: computeStatus({status:'answering', answersCloseAt: X}, now = X - 30s) returns 'answering' (no transition) — X here is answersCloseAt = anchorTick(02:00 UTC + d0) + 7*24h; if the day-7 tick fires at 02:00 UTC + d7 with d7 < d0, then now < X and the answers-close transition is deferred to the day-8 tick, extending the window a day. Same shape for preparing->published and nextOpensAt.
merged.fix: Anchor phase deadlines to a stable nominal instant instead of the tick's jittered `now` (e.g. floor answersCloseAt/publishAt to a fixed daily boundary — the nominal cron time or valley midnight — N days out), or give computeStatus a small grace window so a deadline set N*24h from the day-0 tick is reliably crossed by the day-N tick regardless of jitter.
merged.gate: Unit test on computeStatus with a deadline of anchor + N*24h and a check-time a few seconds before the anchor's sub-hour offset, asserting the transition still fires (or fires within an accepted tolerance).

merged.title: addMonths uses setUTCMonth, so a monthly/quarterly cadence anchored on the 29th-31st overflows into the following month
merged.reasoning: Verified. addMonths (catchups.ts:308-312) does d.setUTCMonth(d.getUTCMonth()+n) with no day-of-month clamp; JS setUTCMonth overflows past the target month's length. addMonths feeds addCadenceGap (319-329) for monthly/quarterly, which sets nextOpensAt (advanceEdition:957) and the cadence-change reschedule (catchups/actions.ts recompute). Ran the arithmetic: Jan 31 +1mo -> 2027-03-03 (February skipped entirely for a monthly cadence), Oct 31 +1mo -> Dec 1 (November skipped), Nov 30 +3mo quarterly -> Mar 2. Concrete but minor: only bites when publishedAt lands on day 29-31 (publish date is effectively arbitrary, ~10% of publishes), and the displayed nextOpensAt is self-consistent, so the only symptom is a rhythm that slides 1-3 days / skips a month. The addMonths doc comment claims only 'UTC-safe / deterministic', not day-clamping, so this is an omission not a comment lie.
merged.repro: node -e "const d=new Date('2027-01-31T10:00:00Z'); d.setUTCMonth(d.getUTCMonth()+1); console.log(d.toISOString())" => 2027-03-03T10:00:00.000Z. Monthly cadence from a Jan-31 publish opens no round in February.
merged.fix: Clamp day-of-month in addMonths: capture the original UTC date, set to the 1st, advance the month, then set the date to min(origDay, daysInTargetMonth) before restoring. Keeps a 31st-published monthly round landing on Feb 28/29 rather than Mar 3.
merged.gate: Unit test: addMonths(new Date('2027-01-31T10:00:00Z'),1) lands in February (<=29th), and addMonths for Oct 31 lands in November.

merged.title: backup.yml's schedule comment claims it matches the catch-ups cron in one quiet-hours window; the two actually run 5.5 hours apart
merged.reasoning: Comment-vs-config mismatch confirmed. backup.yml:32-33 comment: '20:30 UTC == 02:00 IST, matching the existing catchups cron in vercel.json so all the quiet-hours work happens in one window.' 20:30 UTC = 02:00 IST is correct, but the catchups cron in vercel.json is '0 2 * * *' — Vercel crons run in UTC, so that is 02:00 UTC = 07:30 IST, NOT 02:00 IST. The backup (02:00 IST) and the catchups tick (07:30 IST) therefore run 5.5 hours apart and share no window; the 'matching' premise is false and encodes a live misunderstanding that Vercel crons follow IST. No member harm today (07:30 IST transitions are fine), but the false claim would steer the next schedule change wrong, and it is a second place (after C-145) where recorded reasoning and shipped timing disagree.
merged.repro: vercel.json crons: /api/catchups/tick '0 2 * * *' = 02:00 UTC = 07:30 IST. backup.yml on.schedule cron '30 20 * * *' = 20:30 UTC = 02:00 IST. 07:30 IST vs 02:00 IST => 5.5h apart, not 'one window'.
merged.fix: Correct the backup.yml:32-33 comment to state that the catchups cron fires at 02:00 UTC (07:30 IST), not 02:00 IST, so the 20:30 UTC backup does not share its window; if a single shared quiet-hours window is actually wanted, that is a scheduling change to one of the two, made deliberately.
merged.gate: None (documentation comment); optionally a note in docs/OPERATIONS.md that Vercel crons are UTC.

merged.title: gate-coverage's action discovery has three silent-skip vectors for a future ungated action
merged.reasoning: All three fail-open discovery vectors verified in gate-coverage.test.mjs. (1) Line 97 `git grep -l '"use server"'` searches the literal double-quoted string; a valid single-quoted `'use server'` directive file is never listed, so its actions are never swept (line 106's `['"]` char-class defence never runs because the file never reaches it). (2) Line 106 filter `/^\s*(['"])use server\1/` requires the directive after only whitespace; a JS-legal leading block/line comment above the directive drops the whole file — the codebase is comment-heavy, though I confirmed all current action files put `"use server";` first (feed/messages/catchups/auth actions all lead with the directive, catchups has its comment AFTER it), so this is a regression vector not a live hole. (3) Line 58 `exportedActions` regex `/export\s+async\s+function\s+([A-Za-z0-9_]+)/g` misses `export const f = async () =>` and `export { f }` forms; an unmatched export is silently treated as gated. Each vector fails OPEN: a missed file/export produces no assertion, so a new ungated action ships. Corrected Medium→Low: current sources conform, and CI on committed code plus the (main) layout auth still backstop; this is sweep-robustness, not a live gap.
merged.repro: Scratch worktree: create src/components/foo/actions.ts starting with `/* header */` then `'use server'` (single-quote) then `export const leak = async (id:string) => { ... }` with no auth — `node src/lib/gate-coverage.test.mjs` passes on all three counts (file not git-grepped, filter would reject it anyway, and const-arrow export invisible).
merged.fix: grep for both quote styles at line 97; change the line-106 filter to allow leading comments before the directive (e.g. `/^\s*(?:\/\*[\s\S]*?\*\/\s*|\/\/[^\n]*\n\s*)*(['"])use server\1/`); and extend exportedActions to also capture `export const NAME = async` and re-export forms (or assert each use-server file exports ONLY `export async function`, failing loud on any other export shape).
merged.gate: gate-coverage.test.mjs itself, extended; verify with the scratch single-quote/comment/arrow action above.

merged.title: check.mjs reports ESLint and the protocol audit as "clean" when the tool itself crashes
merged.reasoning: Verified in scripts/qa/check.mjs. The lint gate at line 78 destructures only `{ out }` (discarding `code`) and parses `out.match(/(\d+) problems? \((\d+) errors?, (\d+) warnings?\)/)`; a clean eslint prints NO summary (m=null → errors=warnings=0 → ok=true, detail 'clean'), and a CRASHED eslint (config/plugin error) also prints no summary line, so it is indistinguishable from clean and reports `ok ... clean`. The protocol gate at lines 95-98 is identical: `out.match(/(\d+) violation/)`; if scripts/qa/protocol-audit.mjs throws before printing its `N violation(s)` line, n=0, ok=true, 'clean'. Both ignore the captured exit `code`. Real mechanism. Corrected Medium→Low: both gates are `blocking:false` by design (lint line 76, protocol line 92), so a crash never fails the build regardless — the only harm is the operator seeing a green 'clean' label while design-system/lint enforcement is silently off. No member-visible or production-stability consequence; it is a tooling-integrity/cosmetic-with-teeth defect.
merged.repro: `node -e` feeding the lint regex a stack-trace string yields errors=0/ok=true. Or in a scratch worktree add `throw new Error('x')` at the top of scripts/qa/protocol-audit.mjs and run `npm run check`: the protocol row prints `ok  Shape + colour protocol  clean` while the audit never ran.
merged.fix: In both the lint and protocol gate `run()`s, treat a nonzero child exit code WITHOUT a successfully parsed summary/violation line as a gate failure (soft is fine, matching their non-blocking intent) with detail like 'tool crashed', rather than defaulting to ok/clean. The `code` is already captured by run() (line 44); just stop discarding it.
merged.gate: A small assertion could be added, but the practical gate is code review of check.mjs plus the throw-at-top-of-protocol-audit manual check above.

The proxy.md example the finder leaned on (docs 01-app/.../proxy.md:229-256) is about ADDING trailing slashes for an incremental migration ('maintain the trailing slash for some paths but not others'), not about pages 404ing without it. resolve-routes.js maybeAddTrailingSlash (127-128) only fires when config.trailingSlash is true, which it is not here. merged.title: /ingest PostHog reverse proxy forwards members' live session cookies to a third party
merged.reasoning: The browser half is essentially certain: posthog-js fires against the same-origin /ingest path (next.config.ts rewrites), fetch's default credentials is 'same-origin' so cookies including the HttpOnly __Secure-authjs.session-token ARE attached, and proxy.ts lists /ingest as public so signed-in requests pass through with cookies intact. The local (self-hosted next start) proxy DOES forward them: proxy-request.js:30-41 builds httpxy ProxyServer with changeOrigin:true and adds only x-forwarded-host -- it never strips Cookie, so httpxy relays the incoming request headers (Cookie included) to eu.i.posthog.com. What CANNOT be settled from the repo is the PRODUCTION path: on Vercel the external rewrite is served by Vercel's own proxy infrastructure, not this Node code, and whether Vercel forwards or strips the Cookie header on an external rewrite is not determinable from source here. Severity downgraded from High to Medium: even if forwarded, PostHog is a contracted analytics processor, so this is credential EXPOSURE to a third party that has no need for it, not an active takeover -- takeover requires PostHog being compromised or subpoenaed, and credentialVersion revocation ends the window after any password reset/block. Still a real concern worth the owner's attention, but the confirming fact is a runtime observation, not code.

Then confirm the server half: either (a) a request-capture endpoint temporarily set as the /ingest rewrite target on a non-prod deploy, loaded while signed in, to read whether Cookie arrived, or (b) Vercel's documented external-rewrite header-forwarding behavior. If the Cookie reaches PostHog, CONFIRMED. Fix direction if confirmed: route /ingest through a Route Handler (or edge proxy) that deletes the Cookie header before forwarding to PostHog.

merged.reasoning: (main)/layout.tsx:22-26: after auth() the failure branch is a bare redirect('/login') with no next param. The proxy only appends next in its !sessionCookie branch (proxy.ts:256-264); a request that CARRIES a session cookie passes the proxy on presence alone (proxy.ts:149-151, 'lightweight check') and falls through to NextResponse.next(), so a present-but-invalid cookie reaches the layout, whose real auth() returns null and discards the destination. The layout already receives the pathname via the x-pathname header the proxy forwards (proxy.ts:273-274, consumed at layout.tsx:147-150), so it COULD preserve it. Correction to the finder's trigger: plain 30-day JWT expiry does NOT reach here -- auth.ts sets session.strategy jwt with the default 30-day maxAge, so the cookie's own maxAge expires with the token and the browser DELETES it, sending the request down the !sessionCookie branch where next IS set. The real trigger is REVOCATION (credentialVersion bump from a password reset or block/deletion, auth.ts:270-274) where the cookie is still time-valid but auth() rejects it. So the realistic case is: member reset their password on device A, then follows an emailed deep link on device B with the still-present stale cookie -> /login with no next -> lands on /feed, link lost. Real but edge; Low.

Code trace: compare proxy.ts:256-264 (adds next) with layout.tsx:24-26 (bare redirect).

merged.gate: A test asserting the (main) layout's unauthenticated redirect target carries a next param equal to the requested path (paralleling the proxy's B-022 next-param guard).

merged.title: robots.txt, sitemap.xml and .well-known/* are neither excluded from the matcher nor public, so crawlers get redirected to /login
merged.reasoning: Verified there is no src/app/robots.ts, no src/app/sitemap.ts, and nothing under public/ serving robots.txt/sitemap.xml (find returned only nothing for these). The matcher (proxy.ts:320-324) excludes only _next/static, _next/image, favicon.ico, icon.svg, apple-icon.png, manifest.webmanifest, images/ and uploads/, and publicPaths (203-247) lists none of /robots.txt, /sitemap.xml, /.well-known/*.
